posts.title: [MOC/BDP] GG1 Streamlined Electric Locomotive
posts.text: Thank you thank you. And you have a very keen eye to spot that detail. So when the BDP palette was released at the end of June, it was missing A LOT, including the steam engine drivers. They did eventually get added to the palette around the first of September. But that was way too late, I already had the prototype built. When I started my design in July I was stumped. I wound up evaluating every single round piece available in black. Ultimately I settled on the arch windows. They retain the look of the blind drivers but give a lot more flexibility for the frames. Allowing me to keep the build within 6 wide + greebling. This look mimics the real GG1's, the to of the large wheels fall behind the sides of the body and allowed me to keep the height proportionate to the width. You are too kind and thank you so much for your support! In the last round of BDP, someone commented on my "Classic Train" (now up on IDEAS due to the loss of critical parts in the BDP palette, BTW), they said, if you are going to build a locomotive, make it of something iconic that everyone will recognize. That was great advice (but also trickier because it is a lot harder to hide your goofs because the prototype is so well known)

posts.title: Bounty Boat, Lego 6247: A Fresh Review
posts.text: In the decades following Lego's release of the original pirate wave of 1989, building techniques have evolved. Color palette and piece inventory has evolved. Designs have become significantly more elaborate. And it would appear, for the most part, that these changes have been welcomed by the vast majority of consumers. But what about those of us who are overly nostalgic (read: "stuck in the past") about vintage sets? What venue do you have if you are more inclined toward the vintage "play sets" more than the modern "display sets?" If that description resonates with you, then this "Fresh Review" series* is for you! The purpose of this series is to bring a fresh look to older, vintage sets. Specifically their ability to be adapted and reimagined into other (albeit similar) sets. Since the history of vintage Lego Pirates is readily available to all of us, and really cannot be recreated or improved upon, these posts will focus on my own impressions and solicit similar impressions from those of you who read and feel inclined to comment. This post will focus on 1992's "Bounty Boat." When you look at the original box art it's actually kind of mind blowing what you were getting for $4.25 even back in 1992. A very specialized piece in the rowboat itself combined with 3 minifigures? A treasure chest with "gold" and tools to either dig it up or bury it? That's an epic value for a set that topped out at 36 pieces. And if you were 12 years old in 1992 (I was) this set was an accessible entry into the new wave of pirate sets Lego offered that year. The pirates themselves hadn't changed much. They were still up to their old pillaging and plundering ways. But the "good guys" were completely new, even though they were basically just recoloring of the original blue coats. By 1992 I had a few blue coat sets, like Harbor Sentry, Sabre Island, and Lagoon Lockup. I also had the Pirates Minigfigures set from 1989, a precursor to today's "battle pack." But when I saw Lego recolor the bluecoats into redcoats, I knew I had to have both. Bounty Boat was my fastest ticket to achieve this. So let's take a look at this relatively simple set, shall we? Like I said, this set itself is actually pretty simple. It features a rowboat (still pretty new and exciting by 1992 standards) and 3 minifigs, all of which were recolored versions of their predecessors. Getting a treasure chest, some chrome gold coins, and some tools and weapons just round out the package made it all even better. The set itself is excellent value for the 1992 money: Two Imperial Guards recovering some plundered treasure from a captured scalawag, who they've forced into service by making him row the boat, dig up the treasure, and so on. For a small set to include both pirates and imperials is remarkable. The 1989 wave didn't really have any smaller sets that included members of both the pirates and imperial factions aside from Lego 6251. In order to get a member of both factions you had to get either Eldorado Fortress or Forbidden Island. Lego did somewhat address this in 1991 with Lagoon Lockup and Broadside's Brig both of which were mid-sized sets. That year they also included both factions in Rock Island Refuge. The thing is, we've got to consider what $10 USD represented to a lower middle class child at that time. That's a lot of lawns mowed and driveways snow-shoveled. That's a lot of firewood stacked, allowances saved (if your home was fortunate enough that your parents could give you an allowance) and, if I'm being honest, dreams crushed. Even Broadside's Brig opened at just under $9 USD. Lagoon Lockup was closer to $30 and Rock Island Refuge was an intangible $65+ USD. So imagine my excitement when I discovered, first, an all new (albeit recolored) faction from Lego and second, at the amazing price of $4.25 USD! posts.title: Marvel Superheroes 2026 - Rumors & Discussion
posts.text: Thumbs up on the skyline. With all the references and inclusions from across comics, it feels like a labour of love from a true believer. The scaling of some of the mini-ships is laughable—and with the Quinjet or Leviathan, the builds are pretty lacking that I'd just as soon remove them. A minifig Galactus feels absolutely unreal to see and is undoubtedly the highlight of this set. To be honest, I have no interest in this set besides him—and I imagine a lot of the secondary market would feel the same—so I'd like to see him in another set down the road; an Easter egg in a Baxter Building or "Icons of Marvel Comics," maybe? Seems like a great mix between the Architecture and Marvel crowds. I'm glad this concept wasn't split up into five GwPs or collector sets, ala the $40 Disneyland sets—while that'd make it an easier buy for me since all I really want is the minifig, it'd feel especially repetitive to start a new line after two scales of Marvel modulars in the past couple years. Including it all in one package keeps it focused, and hopefully opens the door to, say, a microscale Asgard? (I say this as the Aslume-appointed Thunder Lord, of course.) I wish we could see something like this in LSW. I've already invested into the $300+-a-pop-modular line (as in I own only the '21 Daily Bugle), so all I can do is appreciate this from afar. That said, I like what I see, and if I ever see it on a deep discount, I'll likely buy just for the figs. I don't get any hope for future sets from this, given the sum whole is usually more popular than the parts individually. The purpose for including the niche locations was to fill out the skyline, which typically is not just two large skyscrapers and two short buildings like we've seen in the D2C line. In the latter's case, you could theoretically buy just one and call it done. (I won't because I'm a madman masquerading as a sword online, but I digress.) Thus the sets have to hold their own weight on factors beyond merely "this showed up in a recent project," or "this would feature a fanfavourite character;" it has to look visually appealing as a display piece, have it's own enduring iconicity, and (I think secondarily) feature a broad cast of beloved characters. For this reason I think an Oscorp (with Kaine, Daredevil, Luna Snow and Moon Knight) is the only way to go.

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi @Berthil, thanks for pointing that out! I have updated the link, hopefully it works correctly for you now. You’re right, there are several clock designs that use Technic Curved Gear Racks 11 x 11 (Part 24121) as a frame for the dial, and some, like yours, even use them to drive one of the hands. Yours is truly a beautiful clock, and from what I can see, it carries a remarkable level of mechanical complexity. Huge congratulations on such an extraordinary build! However, I believe my starting concept is quite different from yours. My clock was meant to be an abstract design concept, highlighting the complete absence of a traditional dial and a physical central axis. Making concentric rings rotate smoothly on their own without a real physical pivot presented its own unique set of challenges (certainly different from yours, but very interesting nonetheless!). If the link works for you now, you can check out the Creator Updates section on LEGO Ideas, where I shared a 3D breakdown of the model and the story behind some of the hurdles I encountered and solved. Using a motor was definitely a simpler choice compared to a pendulum or weight-driven system. But I designed this clock for myself as a functional, everyday object. A fully mechanical escapement system, as fascinating as it is, requires constant management and adjustments that I preferred to avoid. Sometimes simple solutions work best, especially when they don't compromise the core design. Thanks again for taking the time to share your thoughts, and I’d love to hear more of your feedback as the discussion evolves!

posts.text: This is how it generally is. With TLG though I'd say it is even worse: They deliberately create new standards either without any backward compatibility or not providing any conversion "items" - in the simplest case, cables - altough otherwise feasible. Yes I know: There was a time when they did that: 9V-PF. 9V-NXT/EV3. And sure, with some tricks you could kill the electronics. But then: Who actually tried? 4.5V, 9V: 2 wires. PF: 4 wires. NXT/EV3: 6 wires. PUp 6 wires. All different plugs. Necessary? Yes sure. Conversion possible? Yes, sure, the electronics inside an NXT upward can >surely< sense what is attached. And back then, TLG made some ... Today, that is history. PUp hubs can control 9V and PF motors. There are no rotation encoders inside these motors, but the PUp protocol is well-prepared for that. Of course, it is. Nowadays, it is so super simple to make such things. The train folks know all about it; stone old classic 9V train motors run nicely on a PUp hub. Any PUp hub. Is there a 9V-PUp conversion cable? No. I bet because it is too expensive to make it profitable. Only for a couple of weird 9V freaks. New customers may not have heard about 9V at all. I get all that. It is so frustrating. The Chinese of course make them. Good that we have an Alt.Brand forum, so people can learn about it. Take TLG's 10V DC power supply for recharging the PF LiPo 8878 as another example. They sold that power supply for +€30! I have a thread on EB about that LiPo: It charges from 9V DC to 18V DC without >any< problems. But no, TLG came up with a 10V DC power supply. "Nobody" uses 10V DC ... why should they. Well, TLG sells their 5V/2A USB power supplies for €34.99 Believe it or not. Tip: On your next trip to IKEA, pick up 8 of their Sjöss 20W USB chargers (€4) for the same amount. Man. posts.title: [MOC] Queen's Castle - BDP 2028 Wave 1
posts.text: Hi everyone, I wanted to share my BDP 2028 Wave 1 submission: Queen's Castle Link Here I wanted to capture the look, playability, and build experience of early LEGO castle sets. There is plenty of room in the courtyard, on the ramparts, and inside the towers to place minifigures for all sorts of play experiences. Inside the courtyard, you will see a well, a blacksmith forge, and an area to feed horses All of the tops are removable to allow easier access to the interiors of the closed towers. For additional play, I included plenty of animals, supplies, weapons, a wagon, and a cog. I was inspired by early LEGO castle designs such as the Yellow Castle and Weetabix Castle. The color scheme came from early LEGO Castle, Town, and Pirate sets that used primary colors, and also from the artistic works of Piet Mondrian. I am very aware that this type of Castle submission is very different when compared to other BDP Castle submissions and most modern LEGO Castle sets, but it was a joy to research old sets and incorporate little bits here and there into this design. posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi everyone! Whenever people say LEGO is "just a toy for kids," I love showing them what happens when you combine mechanical engineering, geometry, and a few thousand Technic bricks! ⚙️🧱 I’d like to share my project currently live on LEGO Ideas: the Working Analog Clock. The main challenge was creating a fully functional, two-handed clock where the movement isn't driven by a standard center axle, but by concentric ring gears driven around a virtual center. The Engineering Behind the Build: To make this concept a reality, I had to solve a few major hurdles that went way beyond "just stacking bricks": Virtual Center Mechanics: Driving two massive concentric rings (built using Technic Curved Gear Racks 24121) without a physical central axle required an independent vertical suspension system for each ring to keep friction minimal while maintaining precise alignment. The "Ghost Hand" Dilemma: To keep standard clock proportions (where the shorter hour hand floats in front of the minute hand), I engineered an internal transfer link—a "Ghost Hand"—that routes the movement from the rear hour ring forward to a smaller front indicator. Single-Drive Synchronized Reduction: Scrapping early dual-motor prototypes, the entire mechanism is now synchronized through a single, compact gear reduction train housed in the rear chassis. Why Share This Here? Eurobricks is one of the best places for deep-dive technical feedback, so I’d love to know your thoughts: How do you usually handle friction and structural roll when dealing with large, suspended Technic rings? What do you think of using an internal transfer arm ("Ghost Hand") vs. mounting hands directly onto the outer rings? If you'd like to see the full evolution, technical updates, or support the build, check out the official LEGO Ideas page! 👉 https://ideas.lego.com/product-ideas/09f27699-c246-40a3-8eea-9a0867d1470f Looking forward to your thoughts, constructive suggestions, and ideas for discussion!

posts.title: TypingChinese — practise Chinese by typing it: pinyin / IME / dictation drills, HSK 1-6, free and open source (feedback welcome)
posts.text: Hi everyone — I'm the developer, so full disclosure up front. The gap I kept hitting in my own study: I could read pinyin and recognise characters fine, but actually typing Chinese was slow. Vocab apps drill recognition; IMEs just guess what you meant. Nothing in between trains the keystroke itself — which is the bit that matters if you ever want to text someone or type an essay. So I built TypingChinese: https://www.typingchinese.club You see the hanzi and type the pinyin — full, initials-only, or with tone marks — scored letter by letter. There's also an IME mode (type real characters with Microsoft Pinyin etc., scored per word), and a dictation mode that's audio only. Words you miss go into a mistake book and come back on an FSRS schedule. HSK 1-6 is built in (5,004 words), or you can import your own CSV/JSON. No account, no ads, runs in the browser, and it's open source: https://github.com/CodeTrainerMan/typingchinese I noticed the Cangjie typing write-up on here, and the Anki tone-colours thread — clearly I'm not the only one who finds the input side of Chinese interesting. What I'd like feedback on: which part of typing Chinese actually slows you down — tones, switching IMEs, or recalling the exact pinyin? That decides what I build next. Happy to answer anything, and if this kind of post isn't wanted here I'll take it down.

posts.title: Online Chinese stories in English
posts.text: Two resources match your method (read it in English first, then find the Chinese) better than a plain list of story sites does: 1. ctext.org (Chinese Text Project) - for classical texts it shows the Chinese original next to a translation, and often links several translations of the same passage, so you can see exactly where they disagree. 2. zh.wikisource.org together with Project Gutenberg - the same public-domain work usually exists in both places, one in Chinese and one in English. Concrete pairs that work well: - 聊斋志异 <-> Herbert Giles, Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio - 诗经 <-> James Legge's translations (both on ctext.org) - 老残游记 <-> The Travels of Lao Can (Gutenberg) - 阿Q正传 <-> Yang Xianyi's translation One warning about the English-first approach: the free translations above are free because they are old. Giles and Legge wrote a hundred years ago, their English is dated and they take real liberties with the original - Legge even keeps the Chinese word order in places. Read them for the story, but do not use them to learn how a modern translator handles a sentence. For modern fiction the problem is the other way round: the Chinese original is usually easier to find than an authorised English translation, so 活着 or 平凡的世界 are easier to enter from the Chinese side than from the English side.

posts.title: 梓 zǐ — how did an ordinary catalpa tree become THE name character of the 2010s? Does it feel dated now?
posts.text: There's a naming phenomenon in mainland China I keep running into: for roughly a decade, 梓 zǐ — the catalpa tree, a fairly ordinary hardwood traditionally planted by the house — became arguably the single most popular character in newborn names (梓涵, 梓萱, and hundreds of variants). The character has respectable roots, to be fair: 梓 was literally the tree of home (桑梓 still means hometown), and it also referred to the wooden blocks used for printing, hence printing plates in old publishing contexts. So it is not a shallow pick. But I'm curious about the felt sense for native speakers in 2026: when you hear 梓 in a name now, does it read as the generational default, the way English speakers hear Jennifer or Jayden? Is the wave already cresting, and if so, what character do you sense filling the same slot next?

posts.title: Not sure if that tattoo was a good idea
posts.text: Coming at this from the needle side rather than the language side, so treat the scholarship as a second opinion. What makes a Chinese-character tattoo read as "native" or not is usually not the meaning. It is mostly three things: whether the characters are cut at a consistent size, whether each character is balanced inside its own square (Chinese characters want to sit in a square, and Japanese-influenced lettering often stretches them taller and lets strokes run from one character into the next), and whether the client chose a complete phrase or a fragment. 歲寒知松柏 is a full classical line, which is the safer kind. The ones that quietly get laughed at are usually two adjectives stacked side by side that do not actually pair up grammatically. For what it is worth, "will Chinese people find this funny" is the wrong thing to be haunted by. The question I would ask instead is whether the same four characters still say something to you in ten years, because that is the only part of a tattoo that is genuinely permanent. The same test applies to the single characters people pick for names. I always set a candidate in a square seal before anything goes on skin, and plenty of beautiful ideas turn into a black blob at the size they actually get reproduced at. If it survives the seal, it survives everything.

posts.title: Native-speaker feedback on a Chinese name for a children's space-builder hero
posts.text: Chiming in from a slightly different angle than everyone else here — I'm not a native speaker. I'm a tattoo artist in the US, and most of my work with Chinese is visual: I look at how a name carries weight on the skin and how much story one character can hold. So take this for what it's worth. Something I don't think has been raised yet: kids' franchises live and die on a single character. The full name will be in the theme song and the credits, but what ends up on the chest, the toy box and the sticker sheet is one big character, usually the one in the middle. So it's worth asking which single character in each candidate can carry the whole concept on its own. On that front, 匠 is the most interesting one in this whole thread. It's 斤 (an axe) inside 匚 (a box) — literally a craftsman's toolbox. It's one of the few characters on the table where the picture still matches the meaning, and "a maker with his tools" is exactly the concept you described. 创 reads as "create" but the shape is abstract, and 建 is construction vocabulary, as Silver2333 said. So my vote is whichever option puts 匠 or 创 in the load-bearing position and treats everything before it as a prefix. 星匠侠 is a genuinely good find for that reason. One practical note from my side of the fence: test the name at seal size. A lot of otherwise fine names turn into an unreadable blob once you set them in a red square seal, and that's the asset that gets reused everywhere — merch, avatars, end cards, promotional art. If a name survives a seal, it survives a toy box.
